name: Bridging Japanese athletes to the US
name_ja: 日本人選手とアメリカをつなぐ
status: Three young players are testing three different roads at the same time. Rintaro Sasaki (Stanford, then the Miami Marlins in July 2026) has not yet played a professional game because of a visa delay. Shotaro Morii has finished his second minor-league year with the Athletics. Shoki Oda said in October 2026 that he will go to the US and was still drafted first by the Yomiuri Giants. He finished meeting ten MLB clubs on 18 November and met the Giants face to face for the first time on 26 November (Japan time). He has not announced a decision. He cannot sign with an American club before 15 January 2027 at the earliest; MLB's labour agreement ends on 1 December with no new deal yet, and a labour stoppage may delay that.
summary: A beginner's guide to how a Japanese baseball player gets to America, and who looks after daily life once he is there: language, food, housing, training, school and visas. It compares three routes (Japanese pro baseball then the 'posting' sale; a US college; a minor-league contract straight from high school), uses Rintaro Sasaki, Shotaro Morii and Shoki Oda as case studies, lists the companies already doing this as a business, and marks where support is thin for players who are not stars. Soccer (Maya Yoshida) is used only as a comparison.
quick_facts: A topic explainer, not a person. Baseball first; soccer only for comparison.
1) Japanese pro baseball (NPB), then a 'posting' sale to an MLB club. 2) A US college, then the MLB draft. 3) A minor-league contract with an MLB club straight from high school.

Stars get support written into their contracts and paid by the club. A minor leaguer gets housing and two meals a day, but an interpreter is not guaranteed. A college player can get a scholarship, but must pass classes in English and may not be allowed to earn money.
Language. Sasaki, Morii and Oda all name it first; food comes second.
Rintaro Sasaki 佐々木麟太郎, Shotaro Morii 森井翔太郎, Shoki Oda 織田翔希
OFFICIAL = announced by a club or league. REPORTED = from news media. ESTIMATE = a rough figure.

rows: There are three roads from Japan to Major League Baseball (MLB). The old road goes through Japan's pro league and can take up to nine years. The two new roads skip Japan's pro league.
https://www.mlb.com/ja/news/rintaro-sasaki-announces-plan-to-sign-with-marlins-via-social-media
The new roads are faster but poorer at the start. Sasaki took a signing bonus of $210,200 (REPORTED) when a first-round pick in Japan would get about ¥100 million plus bonuses.
https://full-count.jp/2026/07/21/post1993010/
Stars who arrive as proven professionals get an interpreter, a trainer and flights home written into their contract, paid by the club.
https://www.si.com/mlb/2024/01/04/yoshinobu-yamamoto-travel-perks-dodgers-contract-mlb-fans-fascinated
A teenager in the minor leagues gets free housing and meals at the ballpark, but daily life is still on him. Morii carried a rice cooker and Japanese rice on road trips.
https://www.daily.co.jp/mlb/2026/11/17/0021042437.shtml
A small number of companies in Japan now sell this 'bridge' as a service: management and life support, college placement, and agents acting as project managers.
https://www.nikkan-gendai.com/articles/view/sports/382543/3
The gap (my analysis): support follows the money. The players who most need help (18 years old, low pay, no English) are the ones with the least help written down.

cells: Nippon Professional Baseball, Japan's top pro league (12 clubs).

The way a player under contract in Japan is 'sold' to an MLB club. The Japanese club must agree. The MLB club pays the Japanese club a 'release fee': 20% of the first $25 million of the contract, 17.5% of the next $25 million, and 15% above $50 million.

A foreign player who is under 25, or has fewer than six pro seasons, counts as an 'international amateur'. He can only get a minor-league contract, and his signing bonus must fit inside a small yearly budget each club has (the 'bonus pool').
The window in which MLB clubs may sign amateurs from outside the US, Canada and Puerto Rico. It runs from 15 January to 15 December. The player must be registered with the league office first.
Each July, MLB clubs take turns choosing amateur players in the US, including foreign students at US colleges. Each pick in the first ten rounds has a suggested bonus called the 'slot value'.
The training leagues under each MLB club. From bottom to top: Rookie, Single-A (1A), High-A, Double-A (2A), Triple-A (3A). Most players spend several years there.
'Name, image and likeness': money a US college athlete can earn from ads and sponsors. Foreign students on a student visa are mostly shut out of it.
F-1 is the student visa; it strictly limits paid work. P-1 is the visa professional athletes such as Shohei Ohtani use; the team sponsors it.
The person who negotiates the playing contract. For MLB contracts the agent must be certified by the players' union.
Management company (マネジメント会社)
A company in Japan that handles a player's media, sponsors and daily support. It is often a different company from the agent.

sections.title: The three routes, side by side
sections.intro: All three roads end at the same place. They differ in how long you wait, how much money you get at the start, and who looks after you.

cells: Be drafted by a Japanese club, become a star, then ask the club to 'post' you. Without the club's permission you wait for overseas free agency.

Free agency takes nine years. A first-round pick in Japan gets about ¥100 million plus up to ¥50 million in bonuses (the agreed maximum). Leave before age 25 and you can only sign a minor-league deal.
The club can say no. SoftBank has never allowed a posting, which is one reported reason Sasaki did not sign there.
Ohtani, Yamamoto, Roki Sasaki, Imai, Murakami, Okamoto
2. US college, then the MLB draft
Skip the Japanese draft, enrol at an American university, play college baseball, and enter the MLB draft like an American student.
Two to three years. A sports scholarship can cover tuition, housing and food. Draft bonuses fall fast after the top rounds: Sasaki, picked 235th, got $210,200 (REPORTED).
You must pass real university classes in English. A foreign student on an F-1 visa can earn little or nothing from sponsors while in the US.
Rintaro Sasaki (Stanford), Itsuki Takemoto (Hawaii), Rikuu Nishida (Oregon), Genei Sato (Penn State, from 2027)
Ask Japanese clubs not to draft you, register as an international amateur, and sign with an MLB club in the January–December window.

No wait to turn pro. Morii's bonus was about $1.5 million (REPORTED by AP; the largest for a Japanese amateur). After that, minor-league pay is roughly $18,000–$44,000 a year (ESTIMATE from 2026 weekly rates).
Years in small towns at 18, a new language, and no guarantee of promotion. Earlier players on this road were released after about three years.
Shotaro Morii (Athletics), Shoki Oda (planned), earlier Kaito Yuki, Tetsuya Yamaguchi, Junichi Tazawa

rows: Until 2020, Japanese clubs had an understanding known as the 'Tazawa rule': a player who skipped the Japanese draft to sign abroad could not join a Japanese club for two years (three if he left from high school) after coming home. It was abolished in September 2020, so going abroad first no longer closes the door at home.
https://www.wbsc.org/news/npb-to-abolish-tazawa-rule-welcome-back-players-who-sign-outside-japan

In 2023 NPB changed its rules for players enrolled at schools overseas: a club that drafts one keeps the right to negotiate until the end of the following July. That is how SoftBank could draft Sasaki in October 2025 and wait until after the July 2026 MLB draft.
https://www.hb-nippon.com/articles/3117
The posting system itself exists because of three 1990s cases (Hideo Nomo, Hideki Irabu, Alfonso Soriano) handled by the agent Don Nomura. See the Nomo and Nomura pages.
https://anishimori123.github.io/News/sports/baseball/hideo-nomo.html

Pay in the minor leagues improved: clubs have had to provide housing since 2022, and the first minor-league labour agreement in 2023 raised minimum salaries (for example Single-A from $11,000 to $26,200 a year).
https://frontofficesports.com/minor-league-players-to-get-big-salary-bump-in-historic-cba

Why agents now appear around amateurs: a sports-business professor, Itaru Kobayashi, points out that an MLB first-round pick can earn a bonus above ¥1 billion and even a third-round pick can pass ¥100 million, more than Japan's maximum for a first-round pick.
https://www.nikkan-gendai.com/articles/view/sports/382543
parts.heading: Rules that opened the new roads

cells: Drafted by the Chicago White Sox in 2023 (11th round). Reached the majors and got his first hit on 25 May 2026. The placement company says he found his college through its tryout tour.
Drafted by the Athletics in 2025 (19th round). In 2026 he was Morii's team-mate and room-mate at Single-A Stockton.
Japanese university, then transfer to Penn State
A 159 km/h pitcher who would have been a top Japanese draft pick. Transfers to play from February 2027 and aims at the July 2027 MLB draft.
Company team, then Boston Red Sox (2008)
The success story: reached the majors in his first season and pitched 388 MLB games.
Never got above Rookie level. Came home, joined the Giants as a development player in 2005 and became one of Japan's best relief pitchers.
Released about three years later without reaching the majors.
Signed during a period when talks were banned and lost his amateur registration in Japan. Reached Triple-A, never the majors; retired after 2023.

parts.heading: Others on these roads, and what happened next

sections.title: Case study 1: Rintaro Sasaki (college road)
sections.intro: Born 2005. First baseman. Said to have hit 140 home runs in high school (the count includes practice games). Son of Hiroshi Sasaki, the Hanamaki Higashi High School coach who also coached Shohei Ohtani and Yusei Kikuchi.

cells: He skipped the Japanese draft in autumn 2023. After a campus visit in January 2024 he asked Stanford's coaches for a video call in February; they expected a 'no' and got a 'yes'.
He asked Ohtani and Kikuchi for advice before deciding. In 2026 he called them the biggest reason he chose the US.

Coach David Esquer promised his father that Stanford would 'take care of your son'. On the visit he spent 20–30 minutes asking Nico Hoerner, a Stanford graduate now with the Chicago Cubs, how to balance study and baseball.

A full scholarship. One Japanese paper put its value at about ¥50 million over four years for tuition, housing and food (REPORTED). As a foreign student on a student visa he could not take sponsor money in the US.

His management is Nice Guy Partners, a Tokyo company run by Hiroyuki Kinoshita, which speaks for him to the Japanese press. No US agent or adviser has been named in the sources I found: not confirmed.
2025: 7 home runs, .790 OPS. 2026: .262, 16 home runs, 47 RBI, .952 OPS, with 45 walks against 50 strikeouts. (OPS is a batting score; above .900 is very good.)
October 2025: SoftBank won the lottery for him in the first round of the Japanese draft (DeNA also picked him). 12 July 2026: the Miami Marlins took him in the 8th round, 235th overall.
19 July 2026: he announced at a press conference in Hanamaki that he would join the Marlins. Signed in Miami on 20 July.
Bonus $210,200 (REPORTED by MLB.com's Jonathan Mayo), below the $239,200 suggested for that pick, and far below what a first-round pick in Japan gets.
His management said Stanford sets no time limit for returning, and that he strongly wants to graduate. He takes leave from the university rather than quitting.

His visa change (student to professional) was not finished before the Single-A season ended. He spent about two months at the club's Florida base unable to join team practice and trained alone. His pro career starts properly in spring 2027.

sections.title: Case study 2: Shotaro Morii (minor-league road)
sections.intro: Born 15 December 2006 in Tokyo. Hits left-handed, pitches right-handed and also plays the infield. From Toho High School, one of Tokyo's strongest academic schools. (Note: his school is 桐朋 'Toho', not the baseball school 東邦.)

cells: After losing in the first round of his last summer tournament in 2024, he filed the paper that makes a player draft-eligible, then asked Japanese clubs not to pick him.
In September 2024 the family spent six days in the US watching major-league and Single-A games and visiting college facilities. He chose the direct road.
He met MLB clubs from September to December 2024; nine clubs were reported to be competing. One report says he valued a fast road to the majors (about three years).
15 January 2025: minor-league contract with the Athletics (OFFICIAL). Bonus about $1.5 million (REPORTED by AP), the most ever for a Japanese amateur.
He said it helped that Hideki Matsui and other Japanese players had been with the Athletics.
No agent or adviser is named in any source I found: not confirmed.
English had been his best subject since primary school, and he studied it because he wanted to go to America.
Rookie league in Arizona, as a hitter only. He had an interpreter, and often wore headphones.
He asked for no interpreter, because with one he felt far from his coaches. He did his own interviews in English and practised new words every day by talking to ChatGPT on his phone.
Itsuki Takemoto, a Japanese team-mate and room-mate who had already spent years in the US; hitting coach José Ortiz, who played nine years in Japan; the club's athletic trainer.
Single-A Stockton: batting .227 with 4 home runs; as a pitcher 0 wins, 4 losses, 15.26 ERA in 10 short starts. He called it a tough year and said his weak points are now clear.
He does not know if this is the shortest road. He wanted to play inside an organisation that has major leaguers in it.
He sat in on the Athletics' meeting with Shoki Oda at Yokohama High School, as the 'senior' who took the same road. 「どういう生活かを一番に伝えたかった」 ("Above all I wanted to tell him what the life is like").

sections.title: Case study 3: Shoki Oda (undecided, as of 25 November 2026)
sections.intro: 18 years old. Right-handed pitcher from Yokohama High School, fastest pitch 157 km/h. Grew up in Kitakyushu and chose to move to Yokohama for high school. Everything below can change quickly.

cells: After his last tournament he flew to the US privately and watched a playoff game in San Diego (REPORTED, unnamed American baseball sources).

Press conference at school, about 90 reporters: he will go to the US without playing in NPB. He is considering both a minor-league contract and a US college. Reporters called it the first case of a likely first-round high-school pick going direct.
He wants to be the best pitcher in the world, and he named the language barrier as the hardest part: better to live in real English while young.
His mother supports the decision, and his coach Hiroaki Murata has promised full support (REPORTED).
The Yomiuri Giants drafted him in the first round anyway. Their right to negotiate runs to 31 March 2027.
A US reporter said he was not yet on MLB's list of signable international amateurs (deadline 1 November). Later reports say he was added.
Meetings with MLB clubs at his school. Texas came first with eight people, including two of its own Asian minor leaguers (a Korean and a Japanese player) to describe daily life after the move.
The Dodgers' meeting lasted about three hours, the longest. Around ten clubs had met him by then.
The Giants made their formal greeting visit after the draft. Oda himself was not there.

Last day of the MLB meetings: ten clubs in all. The Athletics came last and brought their own minor leaguer Shotaro Morii to describe daily life. An Athletics executive called Oda one of the best teenage pitchers in the world.
Oda had already contacted Morii through social media; the meeting was the first time they met in person. Morii's advice: 「後悔がない選択ができれば、それが一番いい」 ("A choice with no regrets is the best one").

First face-to-face meeting with the Giants since the draft; about 50 reporters gathered. Before the meeting, the Giants were reported to be bringing a development plan (how they would train him). No decision has been announced.

US media say a Japanese management company 'with ties to' the one that supported Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Roki Sasaki handles him. No report says he has signed with a US agency. Not confirmed; see the Wasserman page.

MLB's labour agreement ends on 1 December 2026. A lockout (owners shutting out the players) is expected, the rules for international amateurs are one of the things being argued over, and people close to the talks think his signing could be frozen.

Talks timeline: no new agreement as of 24 November. On 20 November MLB repeated its proposal for an international draft (clubs would pick foreign amateurs in turn instead of bidding freely); the players' union has not agreed to one.

sections.title: Life support: who provides it and who pays
sections.intro: The same need is met very differently depending on the player's level. 'Not stated' means no source I found says who pays.

cells: Hired for the player; the agent negotiates it
The club, as part of the contract
Yamamoto's 2023 Dodgers contract lists a personal trainer, a physical therapist and an interpreter (REPORTED by Jon Heyman).
Kikuchi's Angels deal: $100,000 for a trainer and $75,000 for an interpreter, plus five business-class return flights a year (REPORTED).
The Dodgers promised 'best efforts' to make Japanese food available.
Four business-class return tickets a year for Yamamoto, plus one for family.

Clubs with long experience (Dodgers, Mariners, Cubs, Yankees, Red Sox) are trusted for this; clubs with little experience struggle. San Diego is cited for help down to airport pick-up and hotel check-in.
Toronto employs a Japanese dietitian. The food company Meiji gave Ohtani nutrition support through its own dietitian.
The team sponsors a P-1 athlete visa
The club (who pays the legal fees is not stated)
Professional athletes need a sponsor such as a team or league.

parts.heading: A. A star on a major-league contract

cells: Furnished housing near the ballpark, at most two players per bedroom, bills paid.
The club at the ballpark; the player for everything else
Clubs must provide meals at the park. Morii still carried his own rice cooker and rice.
Club: about $710 a week in Rookie ball to $1,250 in Triple-A in 2026 (ESTIMATE of minimums)
Spanish: every club since 2016. Japanese: only if the club chooses
The Athletics employ an interpreter for a Taiwanese pitcher in their minor leagues; Morii had one in year 1 and none in year 2 (his choice).
Morii used school English plus daily ChatGPT practice.
Morii's pitching schedule is planned inning by inning by the club.
Morii has a Japanese room-mate. His manager said simply surviving alone from Japan is an achievement.
Sasaki lost his first two pro months waiting for a visa change.
The scholarship, if you win one
Without a scholarship, out-of-state tuition plus living costs can pass ¥10 million a year (ESTIMATE by Prof. Kobayashi). A scholarship can be cut if grades or form drop.
Sasaki said reading and writing took him two to three times as long as other students.
By 2026 Sasaki answered US reporters in English without one.
He found practice shorter than in Japan and focused on quality and efficiency.
Most foreign athletes are on F-1 student visas, which strictly limit earning in the US.
A management company from Japan (Sasaki's case)
Kinoshita lists what a teenager abroad must handle besides the sport: language, study, food, sleep, injuries, contracts, visa status, tax, social media.
A placement company or an adviser
There are more than 300 Division I schools; picking one is like picking an employer.

sections.intro: Short quotes are given in the original language with an English meaning. Longer points are put in my own words.

https://www.hb-nippon.com/articles/18327
Shotaro Morii (spring 2026): "Learning English is so tough." He decided to do all his interviews himself anyway.
https://www.mlb.com/athletics/news/shotaro-morii-to-develop-two-way-skills-in-a-s-system-in-2026

rows: Morii (Nov 2026): 「やっぱり白米がないと厳しい」 ("It really is hard without white rice"). The food was better than he feared, but he took a rice cooker and Japanese rice on road trips.
https://www.daily.co.jp/mlb/2026/11/17/0021042437.shtml

Tatsuya Imai (April 2026, a proven star with an interpreter and a $54 million contract): he said he had not adjusted to American life, in or out of baseball, and thought it might be one cause of his arm fatigue. In Japan players eat dinner back at the hotel; in the US they eat at the stadium.
https://www.hb-nippon.com/articles/12475
Shinnosuke Ogasawara on the minor leagues (Dec 2025): cheap connecting flights and buses, not enough food, sharing Japanese snacks with team-mates. 「それを覚悟で挑戦している」 ("I took this on knowing that").
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/868357
A pitcher who has played in both countries, Peter Lambert, says everything differs: ball, mound, travel, food, rest.

rows: Morii (May 2026): "So when I feel homesick, I just play baseball."
https://www.foxsports.com/articles/mlb/as-japanese-threeway-prospect-shotaro-morii-finds-his-footing-in-the-minor-leagues

Hiroyuki Kinoshita, who supports Sasaki (Nov 2026): for a teenager abroad, daily life itself can become the fight before the game starts. He names loneliness and the language wall together, and titles his essay with the wish that the challenge should not be 'a lonely gamble'.

More than 1,200 people over about 20 years; about 70 long-term students in 2023. Rikuu Nishida (now a major leaguer); three earlier students drafted in Japan.

sections.intro: Searched in Japanese and English on 21 November 2026.

sections.title: Where the gaps are (my analysis)
sections.intro: This whole section is my analysis, built from the facts above. It is not a finding from any one source.

rows: 1. Support follows the money, not the need. The 27-year-old with $54 million gets an interpreter; the 18-year-old on about $20,000 may not. Yet even the rich star (Imai) said daily life hurt his pitching. The teenager has the same problem with fewer tools.

2. Nobody owns 'daily life' for the minor leaguer. The club gives a bed, ballpark meals and coaching. Rice, a kitchen, a phone plan, a bank account, a driving licence, tax forms and a doctor who can explain things in Japanese are nobody's job. Morii solved it with a rice cooker, a room-mate and ChatGPT.
3. Visa and paperwork is a single point of failure. Sasaki lost two months; Oda may lose a signing window. I found no company that advertises visa handling for baseball amateurs as its main service.

4. The college road has a money hole. A foreign student cannot easily earn sponsor money in the US, a scholarship can be cut, and the draft bonus outside the top rounds is small. A family needs savings or a sponsor in Japan.

5. The language work starts too late for most. All three case-study players began years early or chose the road because of language. A normal high-school star who decides in his last summer has months, not years.

6. There is no shared map. Each family rebuilds the knowledge from scratch (the Morii family's six-day trip, Sasaki's calls to Ohtani and Kikuchi). The Texas Rangers bringing their own Asian minor leaguers to explain daily life to Oda shows clubs know this is what families want to hear.

7. Failure has no service at all. Kinoshita says coming home or transferring should not be called failure, but I found no company whose product is the way back: a Japanese club tryout, a company team, or a university place for a 21-year-old released from Single-A.
8. Who pays is hidden. For almost every Japan-side company on this page the fee is 'not stated'. A family cannot compare offers. A clear price list would itself be a product.

9. An honest limit. The number of players is small: a handful a year go direct, and about 70 a year go to US colleges in all sports through the largest placement company. A business serving only baseball teenagers would be tiny unless it also served college athletes in other sports or MLB clubs themselves.

sections.title: What fans are saying (opinions, not facts)
sections.intro: Reader comments are opinions and are never used as a source for facts on this page. Page read: Yahoo! News Japan comments on a Chunichi Sports article of 20 November 2026 about Oda and the possible signing freeze (444 comments; the first 30 in 'recommended' order were read on 21 November 2026 through the desktop app's browser). Themes are in my own words; no usernames, no copied comments. The first article I tried (Oda's 15 October announcement) had already been removed.

rows: About 9 of 30: go through Japanese pro baseball first. The direct road is too hard for an 18-year-old; players point to earlier high-school pitchers still in Single-A after years.
https://news.yahoo.co.jp/articles/91293d26ebe50644d2e9f91fa4d3121f974eb9b8/comments
About 7 of 30: unhappy with how he has dealt with the Giants. They want a clear yes or no, and dislike the idea of a Japanese club being a back-up plan. Several of these drew many 'agree' clicks.
https://news.yahoo.co.jp/articles/91293d26ebe50644d2e9f91fa4d3121f974eb9b8/comments

About 5 of 30: a US college is the sensible answer while the labour dispute lasts, because he could learn the language and the lifestyle. One reader doubts he could follow lectures without an interpreter.
https://news.yahoo.co.jp/articles/91293d26ebe50644d2e9f91fa4d3121f974eb9b8/comments
About 4 of 30: calm down. Both sides must have planned for a lockout; let him decide in the new year.

https://news.yahoo.co.jp/articles/91293d26ebe50644d2e9f91fa4d3121f974eb9b8/comments

unverified: Sasaki's and Morii's US agents or advisers: none is named in the sources found. Sasaki's management (Nice Guy Partners) is confirmed; whether it or someone else negotiated with the Marlins is not.

A Tokyo Sports article (2024) says a 'skilled agent' introduced Sasaki to US colleges. It gives no name, and it conflicts with accounts that Stanford's coaches found him by video. Left out of the tables.

Which Japanese management company handles Oda. US media describe it only as linked to the company that supported Yamamoto and Roki Sasaki. Tabloid claims that it is the advertising agency Dentsu are not confirmed on the record.
Whether Oda will sign with Wasserman or any US agency: no report says so as of 25 November 2026.

Whether international amateur signings will really be frozen during an MLB lockout. Reports disagree; in the 2021–22 lockout such signings went ahead. In November 2026 Number quoted an unnamed MLB club official who had 'heard' clubs cannot sign during a lockout (https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/872638), and US articles still disagree. Not confirmed as of 25 November 2026.
The value of Sasaki's Stanford scholarship (about ¥50 million over four years) comes from one Japanese sports paper.
Morii's 2026 Single-A games: Daily Sports says 53, Number and Baseball-Reference say 63. The batting average (.227) and pitching line agree.
Sasaki's '140 high-school home runs' includes practice games, as the Japan Times notes.
Which visa type Japanese minor leaguers hold, and who pays visa lawyers. Only the P-1 for major-league athletes and the F-1 for students are sourced here.
Fees charged by Nice Guy Partners, Athlete Brand Japan and amateur advisers: not published in any source found.
The Daily Sports question-and-answer with Morii and parts of the Number and Sportiva articles are behind paywalls; only the free parts were read.
Whether any MLB club has a written programme for Japanese minor leaguers (language classes, host families). Not found.

What was said inside the Giants' 26 November meeting with Oda, and when he will decide: only headlines were seen at the time of the weekly check (25 November US time). No outcome is recorded here yet.
